verses.zh: 约伯接着说：
verses.en: And Job took up his discourse again:[NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew word מָשָׁל (mashal) is characteristically “proverb; by-word.” It normally refers to a brief saying, but can be used for a discourse (see A. R. Johnson, “Mašal,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 162ff.).
verses.commentary:
27:1 The UBS Handbook (p.
481) makes a good comment about the presence of "Job" again in
Job 27:1, when he is named in Job 26:1 (i.e., Job 26 and 27 comprise one
literary unit). Usually the speaker is not named until a new one starts.
The presence of a second mentioning of Job (only here) seems to imply a
disruption in the original Hebrew text.

▣ "discourse"
This NOUN (BDB 605)
normally refers to a proverb or parable but in this context it refers to
an expression of wisdom teaching (cf. Job 13:12; 27:1; 29:1). NIDOTTE,
vol. 2, p. 1135, lists several possible meanings in prophetic contexts:

- oracle

- prophecy

- discourse

- parable

- taunt

but I think "the teaching of the sages" (p. 1134) fits better
(cf. 1 Kgs. 4:32; Prov. 1:6; 26:7,9; Eccl. 12:9).

27:1-6
29:11-20
32:1
33:8-12
34:5

Job does not claim to be completely innocent, but that the severity of
God's judgment does not fit his life!

verses.zh: 神夺去我的理，全能者使我心中愁苦。我指着永生的　神起誓：
verses.en: “As surely as God lives,[NOTE:1] who has denied me justice,[NOTE:2] the Almighty, who has made my life bitter[NOTE:3]—
notes: The expression חַי־אֵל (khay ʾel) is the oath formula: “as God lives.” In other words, the speaker is staking God’s life on the credibility of the words. It is like saying, “As truly as God is alive.”
“My judgment” would here, as before, be “my right.” God has taken this away by afflicting Job unjustly (A. B. Davidson, Job, 187).
The verb הֵמַר (hemar) is the Hiphil perfect from מָרַר (marar, “to be bitter”) and hence, “to make bitter.” The object of the verb is “my soul,” which is better translated as “me” or “my life.”
verses.commentary:
27:2 "God. . .Almighty"
Notice El (BDB 42, see
SPECIAL
TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, A.) and Shaddai (BDB 994) are parallel.
Also note Job 27:9-10,11,13. These are the two titles/names Job uses for Deity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ALMIGHTY (Shaddai)

▣ "As God lives"
This is a curse/oath formula of later Israel. It is a play on YHWH's
name from the verb "to
be." This is another textual evidence that the author was a later
Judean scribe/sage.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY (YHWH), D.

▣ Notice how Job characterizes God.

- who has taken away my right (i.e., legal right of defense, BDB 1048)

- who has embittered my soul (cf. Job 7:11; 10:1)

It is surprising that Job swears by the God whom he feels has wronged him!

verses.zh: 我的生命尚在我里面；　神所赐呼吸之气仍在我的鼻孔内。
verses.en: for while[NOTE:1] my spirit[NOTE:2] is still in me,and the breath from God is in my nostrils,
notes: The adverb עוֹד (ʿod) was originally a noun, and so here it could be rendered “all the existence of my spirit.” The word comes between the noun in construct and its actual genitive (see GKC 415 §128.e).

The word נְשָׁמָה (neshamah) is the “breath” that was breathed into Adam in Gen 2:7. Its usage includes the animating breath, the spiritual understanding, and the functioning conscience—so the whole spirit of the person. The other word in this verse, רוּחַ (ruakh), may be translated as “wind,” “breath,” or “spirit/Spirit” depending on the context. Here, since it talks about the nostrils, it should be translated “breath.”
verses.commentary:
27:3 "life. . .breath"
These are two different words but they convey the same thought.

- life – BDB 675

- used of God in Job 4:9; 32:8

- used of man in Gen. 2:7

- parallel in Job 33:4; 34:14

- breath – BDB 924, ruah can mean "wind," "breath,"
or "spirit," cf. Job 15:30; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT (OT)

Notice it is the "spirit of Eloah," a different name
from Job 27:2, El, but a form of it (BDB 42).

The concept that the breath of God, given in Gen. 2:7, is the
life-giving force that sustains life is common in Job (cf. Job 27:3;
33:4; 34:14-15; also note Ps. 104:29-30).

verses.zh: 我的嘴决不说非义之言；我的舌也不说诡诈之语。
verses.en: my[NOTE:1] lips will not speak wickedness,and my tongue will whisper[NOTE:2] no deceit.
notes: The verse begins with אִם (ʾim), the formula used for the content of the oath (“God lives…if I do/do not…”). Thus, the content of the oath proper is here in v. 4.
The verb means “to utter; to mumble; to meditate.” The implication is that he will not communicate deceitful things, no matter how quiet or subtle.
verses.commentary:
27:4-6 Job compares his integrity to his three comforters'.

- his lips certainly will not speak unjustly, Job 27:4a

- his tongue will not mutter deceit, Job 27:4b

- far be it from me to declare them right, Job 27:5a

- he will not put away his integrity, Job 27:5b

- he will hold fast his righteousness, Job 27:6a

- he does not regret any part of his life, Job 27:6b (i.e., no knowledge of sin)

The implication is that his three comforters (PLURAL "you,"
Job 27:5) have acted and spoken unjustly.

Job's integrity is based on his adult lifestyle (not his youth). There
is ambiguity in the book as to the question of Job's sin.

Job admits some sin

Job asserts all sin

Job asserts he did not sin

27:4 The interpretive issue about
Job 27:4 is, "Is this verse a positive statement or negative?"
Is it an affirmation of Job's trust in God, even though he feels wronged
or is it a rejection of his three comforters' words?

If Job 27 is Job's conclusion to the dialogues then it probably is an
expression of trust. Job claims he has not spoken negatively about God.
However, this does not fit his statements accusing God of unfairness and
injustice. I think it refers to the three friends trying to get him to
admit to secret sins which caused (i.e., the theology of "the two
ways") his current situation. Beginning in Job 27:5 he surely
addresses his three comforters (i.e., Job 27:5-12).

verses.zh: 我断不以你们为是；我至死必不以自己为不正！
verses.en: I will never[NOTE:1] declare that you three[NOTE:2] are in the right;until I die, I will not set aside my integrity!
notes: The text uses חָלִילָה לִּי (khalilah li) meaning “far be it from me,” or more strongly, something akin to “sacrilege.”
In the Hebrew text “you” is plural—a reference to Eliphaz, Zophar, and Bildad. To make this clear, “three” is supplied in the translation.
verses.commentary:
27:5 "right" This same root (BDB 842) is used in Job 27:6,
"righteousness" (NOUN).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

verses.zh: 我持定我的义，必不放松；在世的日子，我心必不责备我。
verses.en: I will maintain my righteousnessand never let it go;my conscience[NOTE:1] will not reproach mefor as long as I live.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “my heart.”
The prepositional phrase “from my days” probably means “from the days of my birth,” or “all my life.”
verses.commentary:
27:6 "heart" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART.

▣ "reproach" This VERB (BDB 357, KB 355, Qal
IMPERFECT) has a wide semantical field. JPSOA, in a footnote, says,
"meaning of Hebrew uncertain." NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 280, lists possible
translations of the Qal as

- taunt

- mock

- scorn

- scoff

- spurn

- revile

Job does not look back on his life of faith with any regrets.

verses.zh: 愿我的仇敌如恶人一样；愿那起来攻击我的，如不义之人一般。
verses.en: “May my enemy be like the wicked,[NOTE:1] my adversary[NOTE:2] like the unrighteous.[NOTE:3]
notes: Of course, he means like his enemy when he is judged, not when he is thriving in prosperity and luxury.
The form is the Hitpolel participle from קוּם (qum): “those who are rising up against me,” or “my adversary.”
The LXX made a free paraphrase: “No, but let my enemies be as the overthrow of the ungodly, and they that rise up against me as the destruction of transgressors.”
verses.commentary:
27:7-12 Job addresses ("Let. . .," a JUSSIVE
denoting a curse), all three of his comforters (cf. "you,"
PLURAL, Job 27:5,11,12).
He feels they have attacked him unfairly. If they want "the two
ways" to work with no exceptions, Job hopes they receive what they
deserve for their treatment of him.

He calls his comforters

- my enemy, Job 27:7a

- he who rises against me, Job 27:7b (MT)

- the godless, Job 27:8a

- you who speak vanity, Job 27:12b (MT)

Notice the questions

- what is the hope of the godless when God requires his life, Job 27:8

- will God hear the cry of the godless when distress comes upon him, Job 27:9

- will the ungodly take delight in God at all times, Job 27:10

- why do you speak emptiness in light of Job's words, Job 27:12

Curses were common literary hyperbole in the ANE. Modern western
readers, who are often literalists, misunderstand this genre.
Overstatements are part of the flamboyance of Hebrew poetry. The book
that has helped me to see this is D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and
Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

verses.zh: 不敬虔的人虽然得利，　神夺取其命的时候还有甚么指望呢？
verses.en: For what hope does the godless have when he is cut off,[NOTE:1] when God takes away his life?[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb יִבְצָע (yivtsaʿ) means “to cut off.” It could be translated transitively or intransitively—the latter is better here (“when he is cut off”). Since the next line speaks of prayer, some have thought this verse should be about prayer. Mandelkern, in his concordance (p. 228b), suggested the verb should be “when he prays” (reading יִפְגַּע [yifgaʿ] in place of יִבְצָע [yivtsaʿ]).
The verb יֵשֶׁל (yeshel) is found only here. It has been related spoils [or sheaves]”); שָׁאַל (shaʾal, “to ask”); נָשָׂא (nasaʾ, “to lift up” [i.e., pray]); and a host of others.
verses.commentary:
27:8

NASB, REB, NET
"when he is cut off"

NKJV
"though he may gain much"

NRSV
"when God cuts them off"

TEV, Peshitta
"when God demands their life"

NJB
"when he prays"

JPSOA
"when he is cut down"

LXX
"that he hangs on"

This VERB (BDB 1017 II, KB
1503, Qal JUSSIVE)
is found only here in the entire OT. Its meaning is uncertain, as you
can tell from the variety of translations. BDB has "draw out,"
"extract." KB lists several different roots (i.e., 5), all
with different meanings. The best way to deal with this variety is to
see Job 27:8a as a parallel to 27:8b (NRSV, TEV).

verses.zh: 患难临到他，　神岂能听他的呼求？
verses.en: Does God listen to his crywhen distress overtakes him?

verses.zh: 他岂以全能者为乐，随时求告　神呢？
verses.en: Will he find delight[NOTE:1] in the Almighty?Will he call out to God at all times?
notes: See the note on 22:26 where the same verb is employed.

verses.zh: 神的作为，我要指教你们；全能者所行的，我也不隐瞒。
verses.en: I will teach you[NOTE:1] about the power[NOTE:2] of God;what is on the Almighty’s mind[NOTE:3] I will not conceal.
notes: The object suffix is in the plural, which gives some support to the idea Job is speaking to them.
Heb “the hand of.”
Heb “[what is] with Shaddai.”
verses.commentary:
27:11 "power of God"
This is literally "hand of God." See

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND.

▣ "the Almighty"
See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI

▣ "I will not conceal"
This VERB (BDB 470, KB
469, Piel IMPERFECT)
means "to hide." It is ironic that Job will not hide/conceal
the truth of a God who has "hidden" Himself from Job. Job
speaks truly about God but his three comforters speak falsely (i.e., in
vain) about God (cf. Job 27:12b).

verses.zh: 你们自己也都见过，为何全然变为虚妄呢？
verses.en: If you yourselves have all seen this,Why in the world[NOTE:1] do you continue this meaningless talk?[NOTE:2]
notes: The interrogative uses the demonstrative pronoun in its emphatic position: “Why in the world…?” (IBHS 312-13 §17.4.3c).

The text has the noun “vain thing; breath; vapor,” and then a denominative verb from the same root: “to become vain with a vain thing,” or “to do in vain a vain thing.” This is an example of the internal object, or a cognate accusative (see GKC 367 §117.q). The LXX has “you all know that you are adding vanity to vanity.”

verses.zh: 神为恶人所定的分，强暴人从全能者所得的报（原文是产业）乃是这样：
verses.en: This is the portion of the wicked man allotted by God,[NOTE:1] the inheritance that evildoers receive from the Almighty.
notes: The expression “allotted by God” interprets the simple prepositional phrase in the text: “with/from God.”
verses.commentary:
27:13-23 This is one of many
graphic descriptions of the plight of the sinner. See Contextual
Insights, C.

Notice the names used to describe the sinner.

- wicked – BDB 957

- tyrant – BDB 792, lit. "oppressors"

Note the list of the consequences of wickedness (remember that this is
Edom and historically prior to the writings of Moses, so how God's will
was communicated to them is uncertain).

- children will die a violent death, Job 27:14a

- descendants will be poor, Job 27:14b

- survivors will die of the plague, Job 27:15a (i.e., death is personified)

- his widows (or the widows of his descendants) will be so grieved they
cannot weep, Job 27:15b (i.e., improper burial)

- others will take his wealth, Job 27:16-17

- his "house" is built poorly and weakly (i.e., "watchman's
hut" was a lean-to type, flimsy structure used during the fall harvest), Job 27:18

- his wealth does not help his family (see separate note for this uncertain verse), Job 27:19

- terrors overtake him like a flood, Job 27:20a

- tempest steals him away in the night (i.e., wadi floods and washes away the
camp site), Job 27:20b

- he is destroyed by the east wind, Job 27:21-22 (this is the personified subject of Job 27:21-23)

- the wind will clap its hands at his demise, Job 27:23a (Tremper Longman III, Job
[p. 320] thinks Job 27:23 describes God's actions)

- the wind will hiss at him, Job 27:23b; AB (p. 173) thinks the subject of Job 27:23 should
not be "men" (italics) but the "east wind" of Job 27:21. If so,
the imagery personifies the "east wind" (i.e., God's act of judgment, cf. Job 1:19).
JPSOA, REB, and TEV all translate the verses as if they refer to the "wind."

27:13 "the Almighty"
See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI.

verses.zh: 倘或他的儿女增多，还是被刀所杀；他的子孙必不得饱食。
verses.en: If his children increase—it is for the sword![NOTE:1] His offspring never have enough to eat.[NOTE:2]
notes: R. Gordis (Job, 294) identifies this as a breviloquence. Cf. Ps 92:8 where the last two words also constitute the apodosis.
Heb “will not be satisfied with bread/food.”

verses.zh: 他所遗留的人必死而埋葬；他的寡妇也不哀哭。
verses.en: Those who survive him are buried by the plague,[NOTE:1] and their[NOTE:2] widows do not mourn for them.
notes: The text says “will be buried in/by death.” A number of passages in the Bible use “death” to mean the plague that kills (see Jer 15:2; Isa 28:3; and BDB 89 s.v. ב 2.a). In this sense it is like the English expression for the plague, “the Black Death.”
The LXX has “their widows” to match the plural, and most commentators harmonize in the same way.
verses.commentary:
27:15 One of my favorite books on
Israelite culture and ritual is by Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel.
On pages 58 and 287 he mentions a text from Qumran of Isa. 53:9, which
may affect the translation of Job 27:15 by changing the vowels only. It
would change "death" (BDB 560) into "high place"
(BDB 119) as a place of burial. The new translation would be "those
who survive them will be buried in ‘bamoth,' and their
widows will shed no tears for them." This helps Job 27:15 to
parallel 27:14.

verses.zh: 他虽积蓄银子如尘沙，预备衣服如泥土；
verses.en: If he piles up silver like dustand stores up clothing like mounds of clay,

verses.zh: 他只管预备，义人却要穿上；他的银子，无辜的人要分取。
verses.en: what he stores up[NOTE:1] a righteous man will wear,and an innocent man will inherit his silver.
notes: The text simply repeats the verb from the last clause. It could be treated as a separate short clause: “He may store it up, but the righteous will wear it.” But it also could be understood as the object of the following verb, “[what] he stores up the righteous will wear.” The LXX simply has, “All these things shall the righteous gain.”
verses.commentary:
27:17 "the just" This ADJECTIVE (BDB 843) is
used several times to describe faithful followers.

- Job 9:15 – right (NASB)

- Job 9:20; 22:19; 34:5 – righteous (NASB)

It is parallel to "innocent" (BDB 667). Job claimed to be one
of this group.

verses.zh: 他建造房屋如虫做窝，又如守望者所搭的棚。
verses.en: The house he builds is as fragile as a moth’s cocoon,[NOTE:1] like a hut[NOTE:2] that a watchman has made.
notes: Heb כָעָשׁ (khaʿash, “like a moth”), but this leaves room for clarification. Some commentators wanted to change it to “bird’s nest” or just “nest” (cf. NRSV) to make the parallelism; see Job 4:14. But the word is not found. The LXX has a double expression, “as moths, as a spider.” So several take it as the spider’s web, which is certainly unsubstantial (cf. NAB, NASB, NLT; see Job 8:14).
The Hebrew word is the word for “booth,” as in the Feast of Booths. The word describes something that is flimsy; it is not substantial at all.
verses.commentary:
27:18

NASB, TEV, NJB, Peshitta
"like the spider's web"

NKJV
"like a moth"

NRSV
"like nests"

JPSOA, REB
"like a bird's nest"

The MT has "moth" (BDB 799 II). This imagery was used earlier in Job
4:19 to describe the frailty of humanity. The LXX combines NKJV and NASB
but omits the phrase about "a watchman's hut." NASB, TEV, and
NJB get "spider's web" from the phrase in the LXX.

It was interesting to me that The Expositor's Bible Commentary,
vol. 4, p. 973, mentions that the words for "moth" and Arabic
"night watchman" are very similar. Maybe this is where the LXX
got "watchman's hut."

verses.zh: 他虽富足躺卧，却不得收殓，转眼之间就不在了。
verses.en: He goes to bed wealthy, but will do so no more.[NOTE:1] When he opens his eyes, it is all gone.[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb is the Niphal יֵאָסֵף (yeʾasef), from אָסַף (ʾasaf, “to gather”). So, “he lies down rich, but he is not gathered.” This does not make much sense. It could mean “he will not be gathered for burial,” but that does not belong here. Many commentators accept the variant יֹאסִף (yoʾsif) stood for יוֹסִיף (yosif, “will [not] add”). This is what the LXX and the Syriac have. This leads to the interpretive translation that “he will do so no longer.”

Heb “and he is not.” One view is that this must mean that he dies, not that his wealth is gone. R. Gordis (Job, 295) says the first part should be made impersonal: “when one opens one’s eyes, the wicked is no longer there.” E. Dhorme (Job, 396) has it more simply: “He has opened his eyes, and it is for the last time.” But the other view is that the wealth goes overnight. In support of this is the introduction into the verse of the wealthy. The RSV, NRSV, ESV, and NLT take it that “wealth is gone.”
verses.commentary:
27:19 The Hebrew is ambiguous.
The JPSOA translates the two lines of poetry as

"He lies down, a rich man, with [his wealth] intact;

When he opens his eyes it is gone."

The MT has "he shall not be gathered," which may refer to
being properly buried in his family tomb. But this does not fit this
verse well, though it could fit Job 27:15.

27:22b "He will surely try to flee"
This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
and an VERB from
the same root (BDB 137, KB 156), which was a
Hebrew grammatical form to denote intensity.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- How can Job swear by the God who has (in his estimation) treated him unfairly?

- How does the phrase "God lives" reflect authorship?

- Who is Job addressing in Job 27:5?

- Who is "the enemy" in Job 27:7?

- Who or what is the subject of Job 27:22-23?

- Why do the TEV and NJB assign part of this chapter to Zophar?

verses.zh: 惊恐如波涛将他追上；暴风在夜间将他刮去。
verses.en: Terrors overwhelm him like a flood;[NOTE:1] at night a whirlwind carries him off.
notes: Many commentators want a word parallel to “in the night.” And so we are offered בַּיּוֹם (bayyom, “in the day”) for כַמַּיִם (khammayim, “like waters”) as well as a number of others. But “waters” sometimes stand for major calamities, and so may be retained here. Besides, not all parallel structures are synonymous.

verses.zh: 东风把他飘去，又刮他离开本处。
verses.en: The east wind carries him away, and he is gone;it sweeps him out of his place.

verses.zh: 神要向他射箭，并不留情；他恨不得逃脱　神的手。
verses.en: It hurls itself against him without pity[NOTE:1] as he flees headlong from its power.
notes: The verb is once again functioning in an adverbial sense. The text has “it hurls itself against him and shows no mercy.”

verses.zh: 人要向他拍掌，并要发叱声，使他离开本处。
verses.en: It claps[NOTE:1] its hands at him in derisionand hisses him away from his place.[NOTE:2]
notes: If the same subject is to be carried through here, it is the wind. That would make this a bold personification, perhaps suggesting the force of the wind. Others argue that it is unlikely that the wind claps its hands. They suggest taking the verb with an indefinite subject: “he claps” means “one claps. The idea is that of people rejoicing when the wicked are gone. But the parallelism is against this unless the second line is changed as well. R. Gordis (Job, 296) has “men will clap their hands…men will whistle upon him.”
Or “hisses at him from its place” (ESV).

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- As there were scholarly suggestions about who spoke Job 26:5-14, there is the
same issue with Job 27:13-23 (see TEV and NJB outline). AB sees Zophar as speaking
from Job 27:8-23 (p. 168).

- The third cycle of speeches is incomplete. Bildad's speech is very short (Job 25)
and Zophar's third speech is not listed. Why is uncertain.

- they had nothing else to say, nothing new to add

- the text has been damaged in transmission (i.e., copying)

- Job 27:13-23 is another affirmation of "the two ways." This has
been a recurrent theme of Job and his three comforters.
